2024 · ACL 2024 · Benchmarks & Evals

ToMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models

8 psychology-grounded tasks, 31 ATOMS abilities, 2,860 bilingual multiple-choice questions built entirely from scratch to dodge contamination — and GPT-4 still trails 20 graduate students by over 10 points, a gap that widens to 16.2 once questions about the same story have to agree with each other.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By early 2024 the "does GPT-4 have a theory of mind?" debate had produced flatly contradictory answers. Kosinski (2023) and Bubeck et al. (2023) reported GPT-3.5/GPT-4 matching or beating children on classic false-belief tasks like Sally–Anne; Ullman (2023) and Shapira et al. (2023) then showed that trivial rewordings of those same tasks collapsed model performance, the signature of a "Clever Hans" effect — a model exploiting surface correlations rather than actually tracking beliefs. ToMBench's authors argue the field couldn't resolve this because the evaluations themselves were broken in three specific ways.

Constrained scope. Prior ToM evaluations for LLMs each probed one or two dimensions in isolation — SocialIQA (Sap et al., 2019) for emotion/social commonsense, ToMi (Le et al., 2019) for belief tracking — never a single framework spanning the many facets psychologists actually distinguish (emotion, desire, intention, knowledge, belief, non-literal communication).

Subjective judgment. Classic psychometric ToM inventories use open-ended questions that require expert human scoring, which doesn't scale to benchmarking dozens of LLMs and introduces annotator inconsistency.

Unintended contamination. This is the sharpest of the three. Because psychology's ToM inventories — the Sally-Anne test, the Smarties test, Happé's Strange Stories — were published years before LLM pretraining corpora were assembled, any benchmark built by recombining them risks testing memorization rather than reasoning. The paper backs this with a small demonstration (Appendix A, Table 4): asked to "give a Sally-Anne test example and its answer" with no context at all, both GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 and GPT-4-0613 reproduce the textbook Sally-basket/Anne-box scenario essentially verbatim, evidence the test itself is memorized rather than solved.

ToMBench's answer is to refuse all three compromises at once: build a framework broad enough to span the psychological literature, format it as multiple-choice so scoring is automatic, and write every item from scratch so nothing in it could have been seen during pretraining.

// how it works

The method

ToMBench organizes its test items along two orthogonal views. The task view groups items into 8 theory-of-mind tasks drawn from the psychology literature — Unexpected Outcome Test, Scalar Implicature Task, Persuasion Story Task, False Belief Task, Ambiguous Story Task, Hinting Test, Strange Story Task, and Faux-pas Recognition Test — each sourced from its own named prior work (e.g. the False Belief Task traces to Wimmer & Perner 1983, the Faux-pas Recognition Test to Baron-Cohen et al. 1999). The ability view re-groups the same underlying construct into 31 fine-grained ToM abilities across 6 dimensions (Emotion: 7, Desire: 4, Intention: 4, Knowledge: 4, Belief: 6, Non-Literal Communication: 6), adapted from ATOMS (Beaudoin et al., 2020), a psychological taxonomy originally built to catalogue ToM measures for young children. The two views don't align perfectly: the 8 tasks only cover 19 of the 31 abilities between them, so the authors write extra standalone items for the remaining 12 abilities (e.g. "Knowledge-pretend play links," which has no dedicated task) purely to complete ability-view coverage.

Every test item is a (story, question, options) triple. Stories are original social vignettes — inspired by, but not copied from, posts on Reddit, Twitter, Zhihu, and Weibo — spanning 9 primary topics and dozens of subtopics (family, workplace, school, romantic relationships, technology, etc., shown in the topic wheel below). Questions are either yes/no or four-option multiple-choice, with incorrect options deliberately written to be plausible rather than easily dismissed. All authors were trained by psychology experts before writing items, and every item went through two rounds of independent cross-checking (worker A checks worker B's items, and unresolved disagreements go to a third worker C), reaching a final inter-annotator agreement of 99.4%.

The inventory is written first in Chinese, then translated into English using GPT-4-0613 (with the correct answer withheld from the translation prompt, so the translation step itself can't leak the label) and manually checked. The result is 2,860 questions total: 2,470 from the 8-task construction phase (934 stories, ≥100 samples per task and ≥20 per ability-within-a-task) plus more items added to complete the ability view, arriving at 1,584 stories / 2,860 questions in the ability view. Average story length runs noticeably longer in Chinese than in English (e.g. the Ambiguous Story Task averages 102.6 words in English vs 164.1 in Chinese) — a byproduct of Chinese being the source language and English the translated one, not evidence the two are calibrated to identical difficulty.

For evaluation, the authors test 10 LLMs — GPT-4-1106, GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106, GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613, Qwen-14B-Chat, ChatGLM3-6B, LLaMA2-13B-Chat, Baichuan2-13B-Chat, Mistral-7B-v0.2, and Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 — under both vanilla prompting (pick an answer directly) and chain-of-thought prompting (reason step by step first). To control for option-order bias, every non-GPT-4 model is queried with the option order shuffled 5 times and scored by majority vote (GPT-4 models showed consistent answers across shuffles in pilot tests, so they're queried once). A human baseline comes from 20 native Chinese-speaking graduate students, paid $15 each, who complete the Chinese half of ToMBench with no extra tutorials — a single, Chinese-only human number is then used as the human baseline for both languages, on the grounds (citing Bradford et al., 2018) that ToM performance doesn't differ significantly between native-English and native-Chinese speakers.

// what they found

The results

Across both views, humans win. In the task view, the smallest human–LLM gap is 10.1 points (Human 85.4% average accuracy vs. GPT-4-1106 75.3% on Chinese, its own best language). In the ability view the smallest gap is 10.8 points (Human 86.1% vs. GPT-4-0613+CoT 75.3% on Chinese). GPT-4-1106 and GPT-4-0613 are clearly the strongest models, beating the second-tier GPT-3.5-Turbo models by more than 10 points on average; among the open models, Qwen-14B-Chat comes closest to GPT-3.5-Turbo, and the authors note that the MoE-type Mixtral-8x7B "does not outperform" the smaller Mistral-7B, which they read as evidence that raw task-solving scale doesn't transfer cleanly to ToM. That claim only literally holds in one cell, though: Mistral-7B leads Mixtral-8x7B solely on the ability-view English average (51.3 vs. 50.8, Table 3); Mixtral-8x7B is ahead on the task-view average in both languages (55.1 Zh / 53.3 En vs. 47.5 / 51.5, Table 2) and on the ability-view Chinese average (52.5 vs. 45.8), a tension the paper doesn't reconcile.

One task inverts the overall pattern: on the False Belief Task, GPT-4-1106 scores 90.8% (Zh) / 88.2% (En), both above the human baseline of 86.8%. The authors attribute this specifically to FBT's structure — classic false-belief scenarios (Sally-Anne, Smarties-style "someone moves an object without the other person seeing") are heavily templated and well-represented in existing psychology-derived training data, so this is read as a case where an easily-templated task lets memorization substitute for genuine belief-tracking, not as evidence of human-level ToM. The weakest task by "LLM Grand Mean" (the 10-model average) is the Scalar Implicature Task, which requires quantifier-based numerical inference (e.g. "almost 1/3 of an 18-player team are goalkeepers — how many goalkeepers?") — a combination of pragmatics and arithmetic that the paper notes is a known LLM weak spot. By ability dimension, Knowledge is the weakest category and Non-Literal Communication the strongest, tracking the same task-level pattern (Knowledge overlaps heavily with the hard Scalar Implicature Task, Non-Literal Communication with the easier Faux-pas Recognition Test).

Chain-of-thought prompting is, on the paper's own numbers, not a reliable win: task-oriented and ability-oriented CoT results are mixed relative to vanilla prompting, and several models score lower with CoT than without it (e.g. LLaMA2-13B-Chat task-average drops from 41.0/46.8 to 39.8/46.5 Zh/En). The authors' explanation is that CoT decomposition only helps when the underlying reasoning it decomposes into is itself sound; if the model's step-by-step "reasoning" doesn't track real social inference, breaking the question into steps doesn't fix that. Appendix I gives a concrete failure case (Figure 6): GPT-4-0613 reasons at length about a hidden-emotion story and still lands on the wrong answer.

The paper's most consequential secondary result is the coherent test: since most ToMBench stories carry multiple questions probing different facets of the same scenario, the authors additionally score each story as failed if the model gets any one of its associated questions wrong (rather than averaging per-question accuracy). Under this stricter scoring, every one of the 10 LLMs drops by at least 20 points (GPT-4-1106 drops the least among LLMs, 20.6 points; GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 drops the most, 27.1 points), while humans drop by only 13.6 points. This widens the human–LLM gap between the top model and humans from the original 10.1 points to 16.2 points — the authors' argument that averaged per-question accuracy overstates how well models actually understand a scenario as a whole, since a model can answer one question about a story correctly while contradicting itself on the next.

Finally, a targeted case study: on the Knowledge/Knowledge-Pretend-Play-Links ability — judged intuitive for humans (93.3% accuracy) — GPT-4-1106 scores only 26.7% and GPT-4-0613 just 3.3% on the English samples, both near or below the 25% random-guess floor for a 4-option question. Visualizing ChatGLM3-6B's attention weights on a failed example (a robot "imitating" flower-swaying it has no sensory basis to know about) shows the model's top-10 attended keywords cluster around superficial lexical overlaps ("similar," "flowers," "smelling") rather than the causal fact (no plant knowledge → can't be imitating a plant) a human reader focuses on — offered as direct evidence that at least this open model is pattern-matching on surface semantics rather than tracking what the character in the story could plausibly know.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

ToMBench's contamination argument is its strongest methodological contribution and its own numbers back it up reasonably well: writing every item from scratch, rather than recombining published ToM inventories, is a real and verifiable fix for the specific memorization failure mode the paper demonstrates in Appendix A. But the benchmark leaves several other rigor questions less resolved.

The model roster is dated even relative to the paper's own December 2024 camera-ready revision (v2 on arXiv, updating a February 2024 preprint): all 10 evaluated models are pre-mid-2024 (GPT-4-1106/0613, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Qwen-14B-Chat, ChatGLM3-6B, LLaMA2-13B-Chat, Baichuan2-13B-Chat, Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B) — no Claude, no Gemini, and no GPT-4o or any 2024-generation frontier model, despite the revision landing after all of those existed. A reader using ToMBench today to judge "have LLMs reached human-level ToM" only sees a snapshot of models that are now two model-generations behind, and the paper offers no results on anything newer.

The human baseline is thin in a way that matters for the headline "LLMs lag humans by 10+ points" claim: 20 graduate students, paid $15 each, complete only the Chinese half of the benchmark, and that single Chinese-only score is then reused as the human baseline for the English results too. The justification (citing Bradford et al. 2018 that native-English and native-Chinese speakers don't differ significantly on ToM tasks) is a reasonable prior but is not itself tested on this inventory — 20 students is also a small n against 2,860 questions, and nothing in the paper reports variance or per-question agreement among the human raters the way it does for the item-construction annotators (99.4% agreement is the workers agreeing on ground-truth answers, not a measure of human test-taker consistency).

The coherent test is the paper's best self-critique of its own headline metric, and it's worth taking seriously precisely because the authors ran it on themselves: independent per-question accuracy hides a >20-point additional performance collapse once a model has to stay consistent across multiple questions about the same story, while humans barely move (13.6 points). That's strong evidence the standard per-question ToMBench leaderboard number is a ceiling on what these models can actually do, not a floor.

baselines

10 LLMs, all pre-mid-2024 releases (no Claude, no Gemini, no GPT-4o) even in the December 2024 camera-ready — the model list wasn't refreshed alongside the text.

contamination

The paper's central defense (100% original items, no recombined psychology inventories) is directly demonstrated by the Sally-Anne memorization case in Appendix A and is the strongest part of the methodology.

what's missed

A single Chinese-only, 20-student human baseline stands in for both languages; per-question accuracy alone (rather than the paper's own coherent-test result) would meaningfully overstate what models can do on a story as a whole.

would raise confidence

Report the coherent-test numbers as the headline metric rather than a secondary analysis; run current-generation models; report human inter-rater variance, not just item-construction agreement.

// bottom line

ToMBench's from-scratch, bilingual, multi-ability design is a genuine methodological advance over recombined-inventory ToM benchmarks, and its own coherent-test ablation is a rare example of a benchmark paper actively showing its headline number is too generous. The dated model roster and the single-language human baseline are the two places a reader should discount the specific numbers rather than the design.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. ToMBench is 2,860 bilingual (Zh/En) multiple-choice questions across 8 psychology-grounded ToM tasks and 31 ATOMS abilities, written entirely from scratch specifically to avoid the contamination the paper demonstrates in prior recombined-inventory benchmarks.
  2. Against the 20-student human baseline, the smallest gap is 10.1 points in the task view (Human 85.4% vs. GPT-4-1106 75.3%) and 10.8 points in the ability view (Human 86.1% vs. GPT-4-0613+CoT 75.3%) — two different models under two different prompting conditions, not one model's line — except on the heavily-templated False Belief Task, where GPT-4 actually beats humans, which the authors attribute to memorization of a well-known task structure rather than genuine belief-tracking.
  3. The paper's own coherent test — requiring every question about a story to be answered correctly, not just averaging per-question accuracy — drops every LLM by ≥20 points while humans drop only 13.6, widening the human-LLM gap from 10.1 to 16.2 points and undercutting the standard per-question leaderboard number as the right way to read this benchmark.
